units.title: Triton programs, program IDs, pointers and masks
outcomes: Map a 1D tensor operation to Triton program IDs, block offsets, masks and memory transactions.
Implement a masked Triton map kernel that is correct for non-multiple shapes and matches a PyTorch reference where the arithmetic is exact.
Explain how one Triton program maps to one CUDA thread block and how the compiler splits block work across threads.
units.why: Every later Triton kernel reuses this mapping. A wrong program ID or an unmasked tail corrupts memory silently, so the discipline starts here.

next.note: Reductions reuse the same program and mask structure with different tail values.
Compare the blocked program against its CUDA equivalent and generated code.

study.title: Triton Programming Model
study.locator: Chapter 14, Writing Custom Kernels with OpenAI Triton through Triton Programming Model: `tl.constexpr` block sizes, the grid function, and one program per CUDA thread block
study.depth: Stop before Accessing Shared Memory in Triton. Descriptors and pipelined copies belong to the atoms unit.

focus: One Triton program handles one block. `tl.program_id(axis=0)` selects it and `tl.arange` builds its lane indices.

`BLOCK_SIZE` is a `tl.constexpr`, so each value compiles its own specialization. The grid function reads it from `meta` so the launch grid always matches the value in use, including one an autotuner picks.
The mask guards both loads and the store. Masked-out load lanes yield `other` and must never reach the output.
Pointer arithmetic stays in elements (`x_ptr + offsets`), never in bytes.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write `add_kernel` and its grid function for \(N = 1000\) with \(\text{BLOCK} = 1024\). State the grid `(1,)` from `triton.cdiv`, and predict a maximum absolute difference of 0.0 against `x + y`, as measured on an RTX 3050 6 GB with CUDA 13.4 and Triton 3.8.0 for \(N = 1000\), \(1024\) and \(98432\).
traps: Using a non-power-of-two `BLOCK_SIZE`. Each block must hold a power-of-two number of elements, so pad the row and mask the tail.

Closing over a Python `BLOCK_SIZE` in the grid instead of reading `meta['BLOCK_SIZE']`. The grid then disagrees with the kernel whenever the launch or an autotuner uses another block size, and blocks go missing or overlap.
Masking the loads but not the store. Dead lanes then write out of bounds on the final partial block.

selfTest.q: Why does the grid function take `meta` instead of a fixed block size?
selfTest.a: The same source specializes per `BLOCK_SIZE` value. Reading `meta['BLOCK_SIZE']` keeps the grid correct for every compiled variant.

selfTest.q: For \(N = 1000\) and \(\text{BLOCK} = 1024\), which lanes are masked and what do their loads return?
selfTest.a: Lanes 1000 to 1023 are masked. Their loads return `other` and their stores are skipped, so only the first 1000 outputs are written.

selfTest.q: One program covers 1024 elements. How many threads run it?
selfTest.a: That is a compiler decision, controlled by `num_warps`, not by `BLOCK_SIZE`. The program maps to one CUDA thread block.

selfTest.q: Why is `x_ptr + offsets` correct without multiplying by 4 for float32?
selfTest.a: Triton pointer arithmetic is in elements of the pointed-to type, so the element size is implicit.

study.title: `tl.dot` input precision
study.locator: `tl.dot`: `input_precision` default `tf32` for f32 inputs on tensor-core hardware, with `ieee` for full fp32 inputs (still rounded at every step, so not exact)

focus: Reductions run over axis 0 of a block. The max tail uses minus infinity while a sum tail uses 0, and swapping them corrupts the result.
The fused traffic claim is \((8MN + 4M)/(2MN)\), about 4 for wide rows. Check the element counts before quoting the speedup.
Matmul accumulates in fp32 and casts once. The cast position, not just the input dtype, sets the error.

The matmul tutorial compares fp16 outputs at `atol=1e-2`, set by fp16 inputs and the final cast. The softmax tutorial uses the `torch.allclose` defaults; `tl.exp` is fast but approximate, so state your softmax tolerance separately.
units.reproduce: On a 64 by 64 fp32 product of standard normal matrices with seed 0, a `tl.dot` loop with `input_precision='tf32'` gives a maximum absolute error of 0.0237 against fp64, while `'ieee'` gives 7.6e-06. Measured on an RTX 3050 6 GB with CUDA 13.4 and Triton 3.8.0; yours will differ in detail. Reproduce the gap direction on your GPU and explain why tf32 input truncation, not accumulation order, dominates it.
traps: Passing `other=0.0` to a row-max load. Masked lanes then cap the maximum at 0 and break all-negative rows.
Comparing fp16 matmul output with default tolerances. Use the tutorial `atol=1e-2` and justify it from input precision.
Assuming `tl.dot` on fp32 inputs matches fp32 math. The default tf32 path truncates inputs, so set `input_precision='ieee'` when the test needs full fp32 inputs, and still compare with a tolerance.

selfTest.q: A row holds `[-3.0, -1.0]` with a block of 4 and a max-load `other=0.0`. What breaks?
selfTest.a: The max becomes 0.0 instead of -1.0, so every output is wrong. Max tails need minus infinity.

selfTest.q: Naive softmax moves \(8MN + 4M\) elements and fused moves \(2MN\). What is the claimed speedup for large \(N\)?
selfTest.a: About 4. The \(4M\) term vanishes next to \(8MN\) as \(N\) grows.

selfTest.q: Why does the matmul tutorial accumulate in fp32 and cast at the end?
selfTest.a: Each K block adds its rounding once in fp32. Casting inputs or partial sums earlier compounds the error, while the final cast costs one rounding.

selfTest.q: Your fp32 Triton matmul differs from fp64 by 0.02. Is that a bug?
selfTest.a: Not necessarily with default precision: tf32 input truncation alone explains errors of that size on a 64-wide reduction. Rerun with `'ieee'` before debugging indexing.

units.title: Specialization, autotuning and compile-cost accounting
outcomes: Design an autotune space of block sizes, warp counts and stages with a key that separates every varying shape.
Gate every candidate on a correctness check before timing, and reject invalid configurations.
Separate cold compile and autotune time from warm steady-state time in every reported number.
units.why: Autotuning buys speed once and charges compile time on every new shape. Without a key and a gate, it silently serves the wrong fast kernel.

next.note: Inspect the registers and shared memory of the winning configuration.
Compare Triton autotune caching with TorchInductor guards and recompilation.

study.title: PA2 Part 1: grid search and local testing
study.locator: Part 1, sections 1.1 to 1.6: tile assignment through grid search over `BLOCK_M`, `BLOCK_N`, `BLOCK_K`, `num_warps` and `num_stages`; Part 1 Testing with `python student_local_test.py student_kernel.py`
study.depth: The remote grader needs a course token. Replace its speedup score with your own interleaved timing against the PyTorch reference on your GPU.

focus: The key must list every launch-varying value. A missing dimension reuses a fast config for the wrong shape.
Candidates are correctness-gated: a config that fails the reference never reaches timing.
First-call cost mixes compilation, autotuning and execution. Only warm calls measure the kernel.
Tune on a representative workload, not on the final benchmark shapes.
units.reproduce: Time `torch.compile(lambda x, y: torch.relu(x + y) * 2)` on 1024 by 1024 fp32 tensors, host-timed with synchronization: with PyTorch 2.14.1 and an empty Inductor cache on an RTX 3050 6 GB with CUDA 13.4, the first call took about 1.2 to 1.9 s and warm calls about 0.1 ms; yours will differ, so compare cold against warm on your GPU. State which interval pays for compilation and what a warm Inductor cache changes, then run the matmul tutorial autotuned kernel twice on one shape and show the second launch skips benchmarking.
traps: Benchmarking candidates without warmup. Compile time then votes for the smallest tile, not the fastest kernel.
One config for all shapes. A tall-skinny winner can lose on square shapes, and the key exists to stop that.
Treating the course grader number as portable. Retime the submitted `KERNEL_CONFIGS` on your own GPU before claiming anything.

selfTest.q: Two shapes share \(M\) and \(N\) but differ in \(K\), and the key is `['M', 'N']`. What goes wrong?
selfTest.a: The second shape reuses the first shape winner without benchmarking. \(K\) changes tile reuse, so it belongs in the key.

selfTest.q: A candidate is twice as fast but fails the reference at `ATOL=0.15`. Keep it?
selfTest.a: No. Correctness gates timing, so a fast wrong kernel is rejected.

selfTest.q: A cold call takes seconds and warm calls take under a millisecond. Which part is the kernel?
selfTest.a: The warm calls. The cold call pays compilation and autotuning once per key.

selfTest.q: Why tune on production-like shapes instead of the evaluation set?
selfTest.a: Tuning on the evaluation set overfits the selection. Unseen shapes then pay for a config chosen for another distribution.

study.title: Debugging generated compiler code
study.locator: Chapter 14, Performance Hints and Debugging Generated Code: `TORCH_LOGS`, `TORCH_COMPILE_DEBUG=1` and the dumped FX graph, Inductor IR and Triton code

focus: The `asm` dict holds `source`, `ttir`, `ttgir`, `llir`, `ptx` and `cubin`. Each stage answers a different question about the final machine code.
`n_regs` and `metadata.shared` set resource ceilings before any profiler runs. Compare them against the launch before blaming the algorithm.
The interpreter runs programs sequentially on CPU with NumPy semantics. It exposes indexing bugs but not races or occupancy effects.
`compute-sanitizer` checks races and out-of-bounds on hardware, where the interpreter cannot help.
units.reproduce: Launch the vector-add kernel with \(\text{BLOCK} = 1024\) on Triton 3.8.0 and read the handle: `n_regs` 26, shared 0, target `sm_86`, `asm` keys `source`, `ttir`, `ttgir`, `llir`, `ptx` and `cubin`, and a PTX header with `.version 8.8`, `.target sm_86` and `.reqntid 128`. Measured on an RTX 3050 6 GB with CUDA 13.4 as the example for compute capability 8.6; yours will differ, so use your own, which `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=compute_cap --format=csv` reports, and compare the structure, not the exact counts.
traps: Adding `device_assert` and seeing nothing. It executes only when `TRITON_DEBUG=1` is set.
Trusting interpreter timing or race behavior. Sequential CPU simulation cannot show either; rerun on hardware with `compute-sanitizer` for those.
Reading `n_regs` from a `warmup` call with one grid and assuming it covers all configs. Any `tl.constexpr` change recompiles and can change resources.

selfTest.q: Which `asm` key holds the PTX, and which holds the final machine code?
selfTest.a: `ptx` holds the PTX and `cubin` holds the final machine code. `ttir`, `ttgir` and `llir` are the compiler stages above them.

selfTest.q: A kernel reports high `n_regs` and zero shared memory. What limits occupancy first?
selfTest.a: Registers. Divide the SM register file by registers per thread times threads per block, and compare against the block limit before touching shared memory.

selfTest.q: Your kernel fails only on hardware but passes with `TRITON_INTERPRET=1`. What class of bug is likely?
selfTest.a: A race, an out-of-bounds access masked by NumPy semantics, or a resource effect. Reproduce under `compute-sanitizer` with a minimal launch.

selfTest.q: Why does the interpreter refuse bfloat16 tensors?
selfTest.a: It has no bfloat16 operation support. Cast with `tl.cast` to float32 for the interpreter run, then re-verify on hardware.

study.locator: Sections 1.2 (cuobjdump against nvdisasm inputs), 2.1.1 (dumping SASS, ELF and PTX), 2.1.2 (listing embedded binaries) and 2.1.3 (resource usage with `-res-usage`)

study.title: Triton lowering to PTX
study.locator: Chapter 14, Triton Programming Model: Triton converts the program to PTX with each program using a single CUDA thread block, and vectorizes arithmetic and memory operations

focus: `cuobjdump` accepts cubins and host binaries while `nvdisasm` accepts only cubins with richer output. Pick the tool by input, not habit.
`-res-usage` reports registers and shared memory per function. Match those numbers against the Triton handle before comparing speed.
A fat binary can carry several architectures. List embedded binaries before claiming which SASS runs.
Triton `tl.dot` defaults to tf32 on fp32 inputs while a naive CUDA kernel stays in fp32. Parity tests must pin precision on both sides.
units.reproduce: Compile a vector-add `.cu` with `nvcc -arch=sm_86 -cubin` as the example for compute capability 8.6 and run `cuobjdump -sass` plus `cuobjdump -res-usage`. For a plain build on your GPU, use `nvcc -O3 -arch=native map.cu -o map`; for the teaching example, use your own capability, which `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=compute_cap --format=csv` reports, in place of `sm_86`. Show the guarded prologue (`S2R`, `IMAD`, `ISETP`, guarded `EXIT`, `LDG.E` loads) and the resource line `REG:12` with `SHARED:0`. Measured with CUDA 13.4 for compute capability 8.6; yours will differ, so compare the structure, not the exact counts.
traps: Comparing PTX `.target` strings and calling it a performance result. PTX is virtual; only the SASS for your architecture executes.
Forgetting `cuobjdump -lelf` on a shipped binary. The running code may come from a different embedded arch than the one you inspected.
Attributing a Triton-versus-CUDA gap to tiling when one side used tf32 and the other used fp32. Fix `input_precision` first.

selfTest.q: When do you reach for `nvdisasm` instead of `cuobjdump`?
selfTest.a: When the input is already a cubin and you want control-flow graphs, register liveness or source correlation, which `cuobjdump` does not provide.

selfTest.q: Your binary runs slower than the SASS you inspected suggests. What do you check?
selfTest.a: Which embedded binary actually loads, with `-lelf` and the driver architecture. The inspected SASS may belong to another arch.

selfTest.q: The Triton kernel is faster than your CUDA kernel on fp32 matmul. What is the first suspect?
selfTest.a: Precision: Triton `tl.dot` defaults to tf32 inputs while the CUDA kernel accumulates true fp32. Re-run with `input_precision='ieee'` before crediting tiling.

selfTest.q: What does `REG:12 SHARED:0` tell you about the vector-add kernel?
selfTest.a: It uses 12 registers per thread and no shared memory, so occupancy is set by registers and block limits, not by shared memory.

study.title: Graph breaks, recompiles and dynamic shapes
study.locator: Chapter 14, Explaining and Minimizing Graph Breaks (`torch._dynamo.explain`, `allow_in_graph`, `torch.where` masking, `torch.cond` limits), Minimize Graph Recompilations (`TORCH_LOGS=graph_breaks,recompiles,guards`, `mark_dynamic`, `eager_on_recompile`), and Dynamic Shapes and Variable Sequence Lengths (symbolic shapes and guards)
study.depth: The book says `dynamic=True` disables CUDA graphs. In PyTorch 2.14.1 it does not: with `mode='reduce-overhead'` Inductor records one CUDA graph per distinct size and warns after 8 (`torch._inductor.config.triton.cudagraph_dynamic_shape_warn_limit`).

study.title: Compiler debugging scripts
study.locator: `code/ch14/inspect_compiled_code.py` for dumping the compiled SimpleLLMBlock kernels; `code/ch14/baseline_graph_break_control_flow.py` against `optimized_graph_break_control_flow.py` for the Python-branch break; `code/ch14/recompilation_demo.py` (in the repository since late August 2026) for guard-driven recompiles

focus: Dynamo captures straight-line tensor code and breaks on data-dependent Python control flow, falling back to eager for that region.
Every compiled graph carries guards on shapes, dtypes and devices. A failing guard recompiles, so changing values look like slow code.

`dynamic=True` compiles one graph for many shapes, but `reduce-overhead` mode still records a CUDA graph per distinct size, so graph memory and recording cost grow with the shape count. Prefer `mark_dynamic` on the dims that truly vary, and bucket sizes when graphs matter.
Inductor fuses and autotunes over the captured graph only. Code outside the graph keeps its launch overhead whatever the mode says.
units.reproduce: Run `torch._dynamo.explain` on a function with a Python `if` over `y.sum() > 0` and on its `torch.where` rewrite, with PyTorch 2.14. The first reports Graph Count 2 with Break Count 1 (generic jump); the second reports Graph Count 1 with Break Count 0. Quote both reports from your own run.
traps: Reading one slow iteration as a slow kernel. The first iterations pay capture and compile; compare warm steady state only.
Closing over a changing Python constant such as a seed or timestamp. Every new value fails a guard and recompiles.
Setting `dynamic=True` and expecting one CUDA graph. Each distinct size records its own graph under `reduce-overhead`; bucket the sizes or mark only the dim that varies.

selfTest.q: What does `explain` report for a data-dependent Python `if` on a tensor sum?
selfTest.a: Two graphs with one break: the region before the branch, a generic-jump break reason, and the region after it.

selfTest.q: Iterations stay slow long after warmup. Which log separates breaks from recompiles?
selfTest.a: `TORCH_LOGS=graph_breaks,recompiles,guards`. Breaks cut graphs short; recompiles show which guard keeps failing.

selfTest.q: With `dynamic=True` and `mode='reduce-overhead'`, what happens when 20 distinct batch sizes arrive?
selfTest.a: One compiled graph serves them all, but Inductor records a separate CUDA graph for each size and warns after 8 by default. Bucket the sizes so a few graphs cover the traffic.

selfTest.q: When does `eager_on_recompile` beat fixing the guard?
selfTest.a: When shapes vary irreducibly and each recompile costs more than it saves. It caps recompiles by falling back to eager.

study.title: Layer Normalization: backward pass and wrapper
study.locator: Backward pass: the `dx` formula with `c1` and `c2` constants, two-stage `dw` and `db` reduction with `Lock`, `Count` and `tl.debug_barrier`; Benchmark: the `LayerNorm` `autograd.Function` with `save_for_backward`, `GROUP_SIZE_M` heuristics and `test_layer_norm(1151, 8192, torch.float16)`

study.title: Custom Triton ops in PyTorch
study.locator: Chapter 14, Registering Custom Kernels with PyTorch (`torch.library.triton_op` with autograd and fake-tensor support) and Debugging Compiler Phases (unknown custom ops force graph breaks)

focus: The backward needs saved `x`, `w`, `mean` and `rstd` plus the launch config. Missing state cannot be recomputed from `dy` alone.
`dw` and `db` reduce across rows through grouped buffers with locks. The grouping is an implementation choice, not math.
Registration declares mutation and schema so Dynamo and Inductor can reason about the op. An unregistered op is opaque and breaks the graph.
Kernel launches must stay on the current CUDA stream with no hidden synchronization, or composition with streams and graphs breaks.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the LayerNorm vector-Jacobian product: \(dx = (\text{wdy} - (\text{xhat} \cdot c1 + c2)) \cdot \text{rstd}\) with \(c1 = \mathrm{mean}(\text{xhat} \cdot \text{wdy})\) and \(c2 = \mathrm{mean}(\text{wdy})\), where \(\text{wdy} = w \cdot dy\) and \(\text{xhat} = (x - \mathrm{mean}) \cdot \text{rstd}\). State which means run over the row.
traps: Allocating locks wrong. The tutorial uses `torch.zeros(2 * GROUP_SIZE_M, dtype=torch.int32)` for locks plus counts; any other shape or dtype breaks the protocol.
Promising double backward. The tutorial backward supports first-order gradients only; state that limit instead of letting a caller discover it.
Synchronizing inside the op for timing or debugging and shipping it. The hidden sync serializes every stream composition around the op.

selfTest.q: Why does the backward save `mean` and `rstd` instead of recomputing them?
selfTest.a: Recomputation repeats two full passes over `x` and risks a different rounding. Saved statistics keep forward and backward consistent.

selfTest.q: What do the `GROUP_SIZE_M` buffers change about the `dw` result?
selfTest.a: Nothing mathematically: they partition the row reduction across buffers that a second kernel sums. Only performance and memory change.

selfTest.q: What happens to `torch.compile` when it meets an unregistered custom CUDA op?
selfTest.a: Dynamo cannot reason about it, so it emits a graph break and runs that region eagerly, keeping the Python overhead the compile was meant to remove.

selfTest.q: Which stream must a custom op launch on, and why?
selfTest.a: The current stream from `torch.cuda.current_stream`. Any other choice breaks event dependencies that callers built around the op.

units.title: The CUTLASS hierarchy and CuTe layout algebra
outcomes: Read a CUTLASS 3.x GEMM from device down to atoms through layouts, strides and tiles.
Evaluate CuTe layouts as functions: shape, stride, index mapping, size and cosize.
Partition global, shared and register tiles across CTAs and threads with `local_tile` and `local_partition`.
units.why: CuTe layouts are the vocabulary that CUTLASS, Triton and Tile IR all translate into. Reading them turns template errors into indexing facts.

next.note: Attach copy and MMA atoms to the partitioned tensors built here.
Compare the CuTe CTA tiling with the Triton blocked program.

study.title: CUTLASS 3.0 design
study.locator: CUTLASS 3.0 design goals, A new Conceptual GEMM Hierarchy (layers detached from hardware generations), Adoption of CuTe Layout and Tensors, and Reducing the number of named types and iterator concepts

study.title: CuTe GEMM tutorial: tensors, tiles and partitions
study.locator: High-level interface (problem shape, CTA tiler, strides); The Full Tensors with `(M,K)`, `(N,K)`, `(M,N)` modes and the M-major, N-major, K-major table; CTA Partitioning with `local_tile` over `zipped_divide`; SMEM tensors with `cosize` allocation; Copy partitioning and Math partitioning with `local_partition`
study.depth: Work through `sgemm_1.cu` only. Leave `sgemm_2.cu` atoms, the SM70/SM80 pipelines and GETT for the atoms unit.

study.title: GPU MODE Lecture 103: CuTe layout algebra
study.locator: Slides on layout definitions, composition and the composition algorithm

focus: A layout is a function from logical coordinates to offsets. `size` measures the domain and `cosize` the codomain, and allocation uses `cosize`.
CuTe stores B as `(N,K)`, not `(K,N)`. Both inputs reduce over their second mode, so read every stride pair against that convention.
Majorness names the stride-1 mode: M-major, N-major or K-major. It replaces the BLAS transposed and non-transposed flags.
`local_tile` slices the rest mode to give each CTA its tile; `local_partition` slices the tile mode to give each thread its share.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, give the byte-free element address of \(A(i,j)\) for layout \((M,K):(1,\text{ldA})\), then compute the `cosize` of the padded shared-memory layout with shape \((128,8)\) and stride \((1,129)\): maximum offset \(127 + 7 \times 129 = 1030\), so `cosize` 1031. State why allocation needs 1031 elements and not 1024.
traps: Reading B strides as `(K,N)`. Under the `(N,K)` convention the reduction mode sits second in both inputs, and every partition assumes it.
Using `size` for the shared allocation. Padded layouts have `cosize` larger than `size`, and allocating `size` overflows the padding.
Treating NT and TN labels as layout facts. They describe BLAS calling convention; only the inspected layout tells you the stride-1 mode.

selfTest.q: For layout \((M,K):(1,\text{ldA})\), which index runs over contiguous elements?
selfTest.a: The \(M\) index \(i\): address \(i + j \times \text{ldA}\) advances by 1 per row step, so the matrix is M-major.

selfTest.q: What breaks if the shared allocation uses `size` for the padded \((128,8)\), \((1,129)\) layout?
selfTest.a: Seven elements of padding per column go unallocated. Writes to padded offsets land out of bounds even though every logical index is in range.

selfTest.q: What do `local_tile` and `local_partition` each slice, and what mode does each leave behind?
selfTest.a: `local_tile` slices the rest mode with the CTA coordinate and leaves the tile modes plus the K rest index, giving `(BLK_M,BLK_K,k)` so the CTA can loop over its K tiles. `local_partition` slices the tile mode with the thread index and leaves the rest mode, giving each thread its elements repeated across the tile.

selfTest.q: A kernel is labeled TN for both inputs. What are the two layouts?
selfTest.a: Both K-major: A is \((M,K):(\text{ldA},1)\) and B is \((N,K):(\text{ldB},1)\). Confirm by inspecting the layouts, not the label.

units.title: CuTe copy and MMA atoms, tiled MMAs and pipelines
outcomes: Select copy and MMA atoms for a GEMM tile and explain what each atom fixes: instruction, types and partitioning.
Build tiled copies and tiled MMAs from atoms and connect each partition to its tensor fragment.
Reason about pipeline stages, barriers and producer-consumer ownership in an async mainloop.
units.why: Atoms separate what moves data from what computes on it. Pipelines then overlap the two, and every overlap bug is an ownership bug.

next.note: Dispatch the pipelined kernel with fallback and regression tests.

study.title: Warp specialization and software pipelining
study.locator: Chapter 14, Warp Specialization with Triton (`warp_specialize=True` on `tl.range`; the book's `num_consumer_groups` and `num_buffers_warp_spec` config keys are rejected by `triton.Config` in Triton 3.8.0) and Software Pipelining and Double Buffering with Triton (prefetch-next then compute-current with the commit-then-wait handshake, `num_stages` against occupancy)

study.title: Persistent matmul
study.locator: Persistent versus naive kernel structure with `@triton.autotune` configs and `proton.scope` benchmark regions
study.depth: Study the persistent structure and the config tables. Skip the CLC variants, which need compute capability 10.0, and run only configurations that fit your GPU.

focus: An atom binds one instruction to fixed types. `UniversalCopy` with `uint128_t` demands vectorizable fragments or the build fails statically.
`partition_S` and `partition_D` can differ across source and destination. The fragment names record which partitioning each tensor uses.
The first MMA mode holds one instruction worth of elements. Its size varies per atom and per tensor, so read it off the atom.
Overlap needs the current tile to stay live while the next tile prefetches. Overwriting it lets the compiler reorder copies past uses and silently serializes the loop.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the tutorial mainloop order for one K tile: `copy` with the thread partitions, `cp_async_fence`, `cp_async_wait`, `__syncthreads`, `gemm` on the MMA partitions, `__syncthreads`. State what each barrier waits for.
traps: The book handshake names `tl.commit` and `tl.wait`, which do not exist in Triton 3.8.0. The real overlap mechanism is the pipelined `tl.range` with `num_stages` over descriptor loads, so treat those two names as author pseudocode.
Adding stages for free. Each extra stage costs shared memory and can cut occupancy below the point where overlap pays.
Copying the 16 by 16 UniversalFMA tiling numbers onto a tensor-core MMA. Real MMAs have their own thread coverage and fragment shapes.

selfTest.q: The `TiledCopy` uses `UniversalCopy` over `uint128_t` for fp32 data. How many elements per thread must the partition deliver?
selfTest.a: Four: 128 bits hold four fp32 values. A partition that cannot vectorize to that width fails at compile time.

selfTest.q: What does `thr_mma.make_fragment_C` allocate, and why not `make_tensor_like`?
selfTest.a: Accumulator fragments shaped by the MMA partitioning, which need not match the global tile layout element for element. The MMA view, not the tensor view, sets the shape.

selfTest.q: The pipelined loop is no faster than the naive one, but profiles show copies and math serialized. What is the first suspect?
selfTest.a: The current tile reference dies before its consumer runs, so the compiler hoists the next copy past the current use. Keep the current tile live across the swap.

selfTest.q: When does warp specialization beat simply adding stages?
selfTest.a: On long K loops where dedicated producer and consumer warps keep memory and math busy together. Short loops cannot amortize the partition.

outcomes: Compare Triton, Pallas, cuTile (Tile IR) and the CuTe DSL on mapping, scheduling and effort for one kernel.

Write compiler-version, generated-code and performance regression tests that fail on real drift.
units.why: A kernel that wins on one stack and breaks on the next is a demo. Dispatch plus regression tests turn it into infrastructure.

next.note: Carry dispatch and fallback contracts into serving paths.
Audit the dispatched kernels with the benchmark checklist.

study.locator: Section 3 through 3.1.2: tile kernels, tile-blocks as the unit of execution, and how tile programming differs from SIMT thread mapping

study.title: Binary checks for dispatch and regressions
study.locator: Sections 2.1.2 (listing embedded binaries to confirm the shipped arch) and 2.1.3 (resource usage to pin down register and shared-memory drift across versions)

focus: Triton maps programs explicitly to blocks and schedules inside blocks automatically. Pallas names programs with its own IDs and indexes block references declared with `pl.BlockSpec` instead of raw pointers, and Tile IR abstracts the thread mapping into the compiler.
Dispatch keys on device, dtype, shape and layout together. Any untested combination must route to the validated fallback, never to the fast path.
Pin the compiler and library versions in every regression test. A Triton or CUDA update can change tiling, precision defaults and resource use.
Keep negative results: shapes where the custom kernel loses to the library decide the dispatch boundary.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write a dispatch sketch for a softmax kernel: fast Triton path for contiguous fp32 rows under 8192 columns, library fallback otherwise, plus a regression test that fails when `cuobjdump -res-usage` registers change across a compiler update. State the fallback condition first.
traps: Dispatching on shape alone. A new dtype or a non-contiguous layout can take the fast path into unvalidated code.
Testing only the winning shapes. Regressions hide on the shapes you stopped running, so keep a held-out shape set.
Treating Pallas or Tile IR snippets as runnable practice here. Without their toolchains they are reading for the comparison, not implementations.

selfTest.q: What is the essential mapping difference between the Triton and Pallas matmul forms?
selfTest.a: Triton names programs with `tl.program_id` and builds raw pointers with strides. Pallas names programs with its own IDs and indexes block references declared with `pl.BlockSpec` instead of pointers.

selfTest.q: A new GPU generation doubles shared memory. Does your dispatch change?
selfTest.a: Only after measurement: re-run the shape matrix, confirm the pipeline still wins within resources, and update the boundary. New hardware does not move it by itself.

selfTest.q: What must a compiler regression test record besides pass or fail?
selfTest.a: Compiler and library versions, the shipped arch from the embedded binaries, resource usage, tolerances, and the raw timings with warmup stated.

selfTest.q: When is the library path the right production choice over your faster kernel?
selfTest.a: When dispatch cannot cover the shape, dtype, layout or arch mix, when maintenance owns the risk, or when the measured end-to-end gain vanishes outside the benchmark.
